newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish export dip, spending rise worrying - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Danish export dip, spending rise worrying - analysts.

text.p: Danish analysts said that economic data published on Friday showed strong domestic growth but lower exports and rising public spending were worrying.

New data showed GDP up by 2.7 percent year-on-year in the third quarter of 1996 compared to an average forecast of 2.2 percent. But it also showed a 2.6 percent fall in exports in the third quarter from the previous three months.
"The question is, is this a tendency that will continue through the year?" asked BG Bank Chief Analyst Frank Fryd Pedersen.
"With this picture of a strong domestic economy and weak exports, worries over the balance of payments are turning out to be justified," he told Reuters.
Friday's figures also showed a third-quarter fall in export enquiries, but Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft told Reuters the downturn appeared to be a blip rather than a trend.
"The foreign trade figures for October show no deterioration compared to the year before so I think that there was a chance swing in the third quarter that gave these figures," he said.
October exports showed a rise of about five percent, both month-on-month and year-on-year, to 25.74 billion crowns.
Friday's figures for the current acount showed the surplus dwindling to 0.2 billion crowns in October from 2.8 billion in September and several analysts have said it may soon disappear altogether.

Den Danske Bank's Joergen Birger Christensen said the most worrying aspect of Friday's figures was a 0.75 percent rise in third-quarter public spending from the second quarter, boosted by a rise in the number of public sector employees.
"It's a pity that public spending is so high when the rest of the economy is doing so well," he said, adding that domestic strength should have allowed spending cuts.
"It's a bad signal to send abroad at a time when there is so much attention being paid to public sector consolidation," he added.

Christensen expected imports, up 1.3 percent in the third quarter, to continue growing. "Import growth will really get going when businesses have depleted their stored inventories," he said. --Copenhagen newsroom +45 33969650
